title: HE TRIED TO BUY THE POWER OF GOD—BUT PETER SAW SOMETHING TERRIFYING INSIDE HIS HEART
paragraphs: HE TRIED TO BUY THE POWER OF GOD—BUT PETER SAW SOMETHING TERRIFYING INSIDE HIS HEART
The disturbing story of Simon the Magician in Acts 8:18–24 reveals why a person can believe, be baptized, admire miracles, and still misunderstand the very Gospel that could save his soul.
He had money.
He had influence.
He had a reputation that made people stop and listen.

For years, people had looked at Simon as though something supernatural lived inside him. When he performed his magic, crowds were astonished. They whispered about his greatness. They treated him like a man who possessed extraordinary power.
Then something happened that Simon could not explain.
He encountered a power that did not come from his tricks.
A power that could not be manufactured.
A power that did not need applause.
And when he saw ordinary men laying their hands on believers and the Holy Spirit being given, Simon reached for the one thing he thought could get him anything.
His money.
What happened next should make every Christian examine the difference between wanting the gifts of God and actually wanting God Himself.
Because Simon's greatest problem was not that he wanted spiritual power.
It was that he wanted spiritual power while his heart remained dangerously entangled with the desire to possess, control, and elevate himself.
And before we condemn him too quickly, there is a question we need to face.
How often do we approach Jesus because we want what He can give us, without being willing to surrender who we are?
That question takes us to Samaria, where one of the most unsettling confrontations in the book of Acts unfolded.
Before Philip arrived preaching Christ, Simon had already become a remarkable figure in the region.

Acts 8:9–11 tells us that he practiced sorcery and amazed the people of Samaria, claiming to be someone great. The crowds paid attention to him and associated him with what they called the great power of God.
Imagine living that way.
People recognize your face. They respect your name. They seek your attention. They believe you possess something they do not.
Eventually, admiration can become intoxicating.
And when people spend years telling you how extraordinary you are, humility can begin to feel like a threat.
Then Philip arrived.
He was not preaching himself.
He was preaching Jesus Christ.
Acts 8:12 says Philip proclaimed the good news concerning the kingdom of God and the name of Jesus Christ. Men and women believed and were baptized.
The attention that had once surrounded Simon was now being directed toward the risen Savior.
And something remarkable happened.
Simon believed and was baptized too.
Acts 8:13 states:
"Then Simon himself believed also: and when he was baptized, he continued with Philip, and wondered, beholding the miracles and signs which were done." (KJV)
Read that carefully.
Simon believed.
Simon was baptized.
Simon continued with Philip.
Simon witnessed miracles.
Outwardly, he appeared to be moving in the right direction.
But the story was not finished.
And this is where Scripture becomes uncomfortable.
Because outward participation in Christian activity does not automatically prove that every motive of the heart has been surrendered to Christ.
A person can attend church faithfully and still be consumed by pride.
A person can speak passionately about miracles and still misunderstand grace.
A person can know Christian language and still approach God with the mindset of a transaction.
That does not mean we should become suspicious of everyone around us.
It means we should humbly examine ourselves.
When Peter and John arrived in Samaria, they prayed for the believers to receive the Holy Spirit. Acts 8:14–17 describes the apostles laying hands on them, and the believers receiving the Spirit.
This was a significant moment in the early church as the Gospel spread beyond Jerusalem into Samaria.
The text does not specify exactly what Simon saw when the Spirit was given. But it does tell us that he recognized something extraordinary was taking place through the apostles' ministry.
And suddenly, the man who had once astonished crowds wanted what he saw.
Not merely to receive prayer.
Not simply to rejoice that God was working among the Samaritans.
He wanted the authority to impart this gift to others.
Acts 8:18–19 records:
"And when Simon saw that through laying on of the apostles' hands the Holy Ghost was given, he offered them money,
Saying, Give me also this power, that on whomsoever I lay hands, he may receive the Holy Ghost." (KJV)
There it is.
The offer that exposed the danger in his thinking.
Simon wanted to purchase what God gives freely.
And the Greek wording makes his request even more revealing.
In Acts 8:19, Simon says:
Δότε κἀμοὶ τὴν ἐξουσίαν ταύτην
Dote kamoi tēn exousian tautēn.
A close translation is:
"Give me also this authority."
The important word is ἐξουσίαν (exousian), the accusative form of exousia, meaning authority, right, or delegated power.
Simon was not merely asking to witness another miracle.
He was asking for the authority associated with the apostles' ministry.
He wanted to be able to lay hands on people so that they would receive the Holy Spirit.
But the Holy Spirit is not a commodity.
The Spirit is not merchandise.
The Spirit is not a force that human beings can own and distribute according to their personal ambitions.
God is sovereign over His gifts.
And no amount of money can turn divine grace into private property.
This is why Simon's request was so serious.
He had brought the logic of his former world into the presence of the living God.
He understood influence.
He understood reputation.
He understood the usefulness of extraordinary power.
But he had not yet understood the holiness of what he was asking for.
And then Peter answered him.
Not with polite encouragement.
Not with a business proposal.
Not with a negotiation.
With a rebuke so severe that it has echoed through nearly two thousand years of church history.
Acts 8:20 declares:
"Thy money perish with thee, because thou hast thought that the gift of God may be purchased with money." (KJV)
The Greek begins:
Τὸ ἀργύριόν σου σὺν σοὶ εἴη εἰς ἀπώλειαν
To argyrion sou syn soi eiē eis apōleian.
The sense is:
"May your silver perish with you."
The word ἀπώλειαν (apōleian) carries the meaning of destruction, ruin, or perdition.
Peter was not offering a casual correction about poor financial judgment.
He was confronting a spiritually destructive misunderstanding of God.
Simon's money was not inherently the problem.
His heart was.
Money can feed the hungry.
Money can provide for families.
But money cannot purchase forgiveness.
It cannot purchase salvation.
It cannot purchase the Holy Spirit.
It cannot purchase divine favor.
And it cannot purchase authority over the things of God.
There is a reason this passage later became associated with the word simony—the buying or selling of spiritual offices, privileges, or sacred things.
The tragedy of Simon's offer was not simply that he placed money on the table.
It was that he approached God's gift as though it were something he could acquire and control.
And this is where the story reaches beyond ancient Samaria.
Because not everyone who tries to bargain with God uses silver.
Sometimes we try to bargain with obedience.
"Lord, I have been faithful. Why haven't You given me what I asked for?"
Sometimes we bargain with generosity.
"Lord, I gave so much. Surely You owe me a breakthrough."
Sometimes we bargain with religious activity.
"Lord, I serve. I pray. I attend church. Why is my life still difficult?"
And sometimes, without realizing it, we begin treating God as though He were obligated to reward our performance on our preferred schedule.
But grace is not wages.
The Gospel is not a marketplace.
Jesus Christ did not go to the cross to establish a spiritual business arrangement with sinners.
He went to the cross to redeem people who could never afford their own salvation.
Ephesians 2:8–9 says:
"For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God:
Not of works, lest any man should boast." (KJV)
The Greek word for grace is χάρις (charis).
It speaks of favor and gracious generosity.
In the context of salvation, it reminds us that redemption begins with God's goodness, not human purchasing power.
We do not bring enough righteousness to buy acceptance.
We do not bring enough religious achievements to erase guilt.
We do not bring enough money to settle the debt of sin.
We come to Jesus Christ empty-handed, trusting the Savior who gave Himself for us.
And that is what makes Simon's story so piercing.
He was standing near the testimony of a Gospel purchased for sinners by Christ's blood, yet he tried to introduce another payment.
His silver.
Peter continued in Acts 8:21:
"Thou hast neither part nor lot in this matter: for thy heart is not right in the sight of God." (KJV)
Notice where Peter directs the confrontation.
Not Simon's appearance.
Not his reputation.
Not his social status.
His heart.
The Greek expression includes:
ἡ γὰρ καρδία σου οὐκ ἔστιν εὐθεῖα ἔναντι τοῦ θεοῦ
Hē gar kardia sou ouk estin eutheia enanti tou theou.
"For your heart is not right before God."
The word καρδία (kardia) refers to the heart, the inner center of human thought, desire, and intention.
The word εὐθεῖα (eutheia) means straight or upright.
Peter was exposing a heart that was not upright before God.
And perhaps that is the most frightening part of this entire account.
Simon had been close to genuine spiritual activity.
He had witnessed the preaching of Christ.
He had been baptized.
He had remained near Philip.
Yet Peter identified a serious disorder within him.

This passage does not give us permission to declare with certainty the eternal destiny of everyone whose motives are mixed. Nor does it settle every theological debate concerning the nature of Simon's earlier belief.
But it does establish something unmistakable.
Religious proximity is not the same thing as a heart made right before God.
You can be near a sermon and still resist its message.
You can be moved by worship and still refuse repentance.
You can admire Jesus and still cling to the throne of your own life.
And you can be fascinated by spiritual power while avoiding the surrender that discipleship requires.
That is a dangerous place to live.
Not because Jesus is unwilling to receive repentant sinners.
But because pride can convince us that we need everything from God except correction.
Then Peter says something that changes the direction of the entire encounter.
Acts 8:22:
"Repent therefore of this thy wickedness, and pray God, if perhaps the thought of thine heart may be forgiven thee." (KJV)
Peter did not simply expose Simon's sin and walk away.
He called him to repent.
That matters.
Because even in the middle of a severe rebuke, Simon was being directed toward the mercy of God.
The Greek word is μετανόησον (metanoēson), from metanoeō, meaning to repent—to change one's mind or turn from a sinful course.
Biblical repentance is more than feeling embarrassed after being confronted.
It is not merely regretting that someone discovered what we were doing.
It is a genuine turning toward God that involves acknowledging sin and abandoning our rebellion.
Repentance does not purchase forgiveness.
It is the fitting response of a sinner confronted by God's truth and mercy.
Peter's words, "if perhaps," express the seriousness of Simon's condition. They do not mean that sincere repentance is powerless or that Christ is reluctant to forgive those who truly come to Him.
Scripture assures us in 1 John 1:9:
"If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness." (KJV)
That promise rests upon the saving work of Jesus Christ.
And here is the hope Simon needed.
The very God whose gift he tried to buy was the God before whom he could repent.
He could not purchase the Spirit.
But he was being told to seek God's mercy.
He could not negotiate for spiritual authority.
But he was being summoned to turn away from wickedness.
He could not save himself with silver.
But the Gospel proclaimed a Savior who gave His own life for sinners.
This is the difference between religion built around human control and the Gospel of Jesus Christ.
Religion can become obsessed with what we can achieve, possess, or display.
The Gospel announces what Christ has accomplished through His death and resurrection.
Religion distorted by pride asks, "How can I become greater?"
The Gospel teaches us to confess, "He must increase, but I must decrease." (John 3:30, KJV)
And this is why the cross destroys every illusion that salvation can be bought.
First Peter 1:18–19 says:
"Forasmuch as ye know that ye were not redeemed with corruptible things, as silver and gold, from your vain conversation received by tradition from your fathers;
But with the precious blood of Christ, as of a lamb without blemish and without spot." (KJV)
Simon offered silver for spiritual authority.
Jesus shed His blood to redeem sinners.
Do you see the contrast?
One man tried to acquire God's gift through money.
The Son of God gave Himself so that undeserving people could receive mercy through faith.
And there is no amount of earthly wealth that can stand beside that sacrifice.
Perhaps you have never tried to purchase a spiritual gift.
Perhaps you have never sought influence in a church.
Perhaps you have never wanted a platform or a ministry title.
But have you ever secretly wanted people to admire your spirituality more than you wanted them to see Jesus?
Have you ever felt jealous when someone else was entrusted with an opportunity you wanted?
Have you ever measured God's love by how quickly He answered your prayers?
Have you ever used Christian language to hide motives you were afraid to confess?
These are not questions meant to crush the sincere believer.
They are invitations to let the Word of God search places that outward religion cannot reach.
Because the Gospel does not merely address our visible behavior.
It reaches into our motives.
It exposes pride.
It confronts greed.
It challenges our craving for recognition.
And it calls us to a deeper freedom than the freedom of getting everything we want.
The freedom of belonging to Jesus.
Peter's next words were equally severe.
Acts 8:23:
"For I perceive that thou art in the gall of bitterness, and in the bond of iniquity." (KJV)
This was a diagnosis of spiritual bondage, not a description of someone who simply made an innocent mistake.
The Greek phrase σύνδεσμον ἀδικίας (syndesmon adikias) conveys a bond or binding connection with unrighteousness.
Simon had sought the ability to exercise spiritual authority, yet Peter described him as bound by sin.
What a devastating reversal.
The man who wanted power needed deliverance from his own wickedness.
The man who wanted authority needed to submit to God.
The man who wanted to give the Holy Spirit to others needed to confront the condition of his own heart.
And perhaps someone reading this understands that contradiction more deeply than they want to admit.
You have spent years trying to look strong while privately feeling enslaved.
You know how to encourage everyone else, but you are afraid to admit how far your own heart has drifted.
You can quote verses about freedom while struggling with bitterness.
You can speak about grace while carrying secret guilt.
You can look spiritually composed while feeling desperately far from God.
And somewhere along the way, you learned how to maintain the appearance of faith without being honest about the condition of your soul.
But Jesus did not come to rescue an image.
He came to save sinners.
You do not have to manufacture an impressive spiritual reputation before you can confess your need for mercy.
You do not have to pretend your motives have always been pure.
You do not have to defend what the Holy Spirit is exposing through Scripture.
You can repent.
You can confess.
You can come to Christ.
And you can begin again in the grace that you could never purchase.
Then we reach Simon's final recorded words in this encounter.
Acts 8:24:
"Then answered Simon, and said, Pray ye to the Lord for me, that none of these things which ye have spoken come upon me." (KJV)
It is a startling ending.
Simon asks Peter and John to pray for him.
But notice what the passage does not tell us.
It does not explicitly say that Simon repented.
It does not explicitly say that his heart was transformed.
It does not reveal his final eternal condition.
Some later Christian traditions make further claims about Simon, but Acts 8 itself ends this confrontation without confirming the outcome of his repentance.
We must not pretend Scripture says more than it actually says.
His request could reflect genuine fear and a desire for help. Yet the text leaves us unable to determine whether he moved from fear of consequences to true repentance before God.
And that uncertainty is part of what makes the passage so haunting.
We hear the rebuke.
We hear the call to repent.
We hear Simon ask for prayer.
But we are not shown the final condition of his heart.
It is as though the story leaves us standing before a mirror.
Because the question is no longer only what Simon did next.
The question is what we will do with the truth we have heard.
Will we merely become frightened of consequences?
Or will we turn to Jesus Christ?
Will we ask God only to remove the pain our sins have caused?
Or will we ask Him to cleanse the desires that led us into sin?
Will we keep seeking spiritual experiences that impress other people?
Or will we seek to know, love, and obey the Savior?
There is an enormous difference between wanting God to rescue your reputation and wanting God to redeem your heart.
And if this story has exposed something in you, do not rush past that moment.
Do not cover it with religious words.
Do not assume conviction means God has abandoned you.
The call to repent is serious, but it directs us toward the Savior who receives those who come to Him in faith.
Jesus said in John 6:37:
"Him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out." (KJV)
That is not a promise that sin does not matter.
It is a promise that Christ is a sufficient Savior for those who come to Him.
His mercy is not for sale.
His forgiveness is not reserved for the wealthy.
His grace is not limited to people with impressive spiritual histories.
At the cross, Jesus bore the penalty of sin.
In His resurrection, He triumphed over death.
And through Him, sinners are called to repent, believe, and receive the gift of eternal life.
This is why the Gospel is not merely the story of people becoming better versions of themselves.
It is the announcement that Jesus Christ saves the guilty, reconciles sinners to God, and transforms lives through His grace.
Not because sin was harmless.
Not because judgment was imaginary.
Not because repentance was unnecessary.
But because Jesus Christ is mighty to save.
Simon's story warns us never to confuse financial giving with spiritual purchasing.

Supporting a Gospel ministry can be an act of worship, generosity, and partnership in the work of making Christ known. But it must never be presented as a payment for God's favor, a substitute for obedience, or a guarantee of spiritual blessings.
God does not need your money to remain God.
And you do not need to pay a ministry to prove that you love Jesus.
But if God has used this message to strengthen your faith, confront your heart, or draw you closer to His Word, you can choose to help make this kind of biblical teaching available to others.
That is the heart behind Gospel Warrior.
We want the person hiding behind a smile to encounter the truth of Christ.
We want the exhausted believer to remember that grace is real.

We want the struggling father, the wounded mother, the young Christian battling temptation, and the person who has not opened a Bible in years to discover that Jesus is still calling sinners to repentance and faith.
We want biblical truth to travel farther than our individual voices could ever carry it.
Not to buy the blessing of God.
But out of gratitude for the grace He has already given.
Not because generosity earns salvation.
But because those who have received freely can choose to give generously.
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us:
"Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver." (KJV)
Notice those words.
Not grudgingly.
Not of necessity.
A cheerful giver.
Christian generosity should be rooted in freedom, sincerity, and love—not guilt, pressure, or fear.
These products are not spiritual rewards, and the discount is not a measure of God's approval. They are simply a way to express appreciation to those who help sustain the ministry.
The Word of God should never be reduced to a sales pitch.
Our desire is that these resources help you study Scripture, grow in discernment, strengthen your prayer life, and become more firmly rooted in the Gospel.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God.
Not because every Christian must support this particular page.
But because someone in your circle may need to hear this message.
Someone may be chasing spiritual experiences without knowing the Savior.
Someone may be exhausted from trying to earn God's acceptance.
Someone may be secretly struggling with pride, jealousy, religious performance, or guilt.
Someone may have been taught that a financial gift could purchase a miracle.
And someone may need to hear, perhaps for the first time, that forgiveness is received through Jesus Christ—not purchased through human effort.
And please, do not leave this story as merely something you read.
Let it become a moment of honest reflection.
If you recognize that you have sometimes wanted God's blessings more than God's presence, you are not alone in needing to repent.
If you have struggled with pride or the desire to be recognized, bring that struggle into the light.
If you have been trying to earn forgiveness through religious performance, hear again the good news that Christ is sufficient.
Or tell us what part of Simon's story challenged you most.
It does not need to reveal private details.
It can be a Scripture, a testimony, a question, or a sincere request for prayer.
Because behind every comment is a real person, and real people need the truth and grace of Jesus Christ.
And now, before you leave this story, return with me to that moment in Samaria.
Simon is standing before Peter.
He has seen the Spirit's work.
He has offered his money.
His motives have been confronted.
And the apostle has told him to repent.
Imagine the silence after those words.
The silver that seemed so useful only moments earlier is suddenly worthless for the thing Simon truly needs.
He cannot buy a clean heart.
He cannot purchase reconciliation with God.
He cannot negotiate his way into righteousness.
He can only turn toward the mercy of the Lord.
And that is where this ancient account reaches into our lives.
Because eventually every person must face the limits of what earthly things can provide.
Your reputation cannot forgive your sins.
Your achievements cannot cleanse your conscience.
Your possessions cannot reconcile you to God.
Your religious activity cannot replace faith in Christ.
And the admiration of a thousand people cannot make a heart right before the Lord.
But Jesus can save.
He can forgive the sinner who repents and believes.
He can transform the proud.
He can restore the wandering.
He can teach us to love holiness more than applause and obedience more than influence.
He can take a life marked by shame and make it a testimony of grace.
That does not mean every consequence disappears.
It does not mean the past never happened.
It means the past does not have to be the final word over a person redeemed by Christ.
And perhaps that is the message you needed tonight.
You do not need to impress Jesus.
You need to come to Him.
You do not need to purchase His mercy.
You need to trust His finished work.
You do not need to pretend that your heart has always been pure.
You need to bring your sin into the light and repent.
The same Gospel that exposes our wickedness also reveals the Savior who died for sinners.
And that is why we must never turn God's grace into a transaction.
Simon asked, "How much will it cost me to possess this power?"
The Gospel calls us to ask a far greater question.
"What has Jesus Christ already done to save someone like me?"
And the answer is found at Calvary.
Not in silver.
Not in gold.
But in the precious blood of the Lamb.
The tragedy is not that you have nothing with which to buy God's grace. The tragedy would be walking away from the Savior who offers mercy that money could never purchase.
